e: note:'Kazakhstan CPC Blend pipes via the Caspian Pipeline Consortium to Novorossiysk on the Black Sea, then Suezmax tankers transit the Bosphorus into the Mediterranean and clear Gibraltar to UK refineries. e: note:'The Strait of Hormuz is the mandatory exit for all crude loaded inside the Persian Gulf. For the UK, only Saudi Arabia (5%) and Iraq (3%) transit Hormuz, totalling 8% of crude imports. Compare: China 44%, South Korea over 70%, Japan over 80%. Gulf crude then continues through the Arabian Sea to Bab el-Mandeb and the Suez Canal before reaching Mediterranean and Gibraltar.'

e: note:'Bab el-Mandeb (Gate of Tears) and the Suez Canal form a sequential double chokepoint for all Arabian Sea traffic bound for the Mediterranean. Gulf crude exits Hormuz, crosses the Arabian Sea, transits Bab el-Mandeb into the Red Sea, then passes through the Suez Canal (193km, single-lane in parts) before emerging into the Mediterranean. Either node can independently block the route: Bab el-Mandeb through military interdiction, Suez through political closure or accident (as in 2021). Since late 2023, Houthi attacks have made Bab el-Mandeb the most actively contested maritime chokepoint in the world; most tankers have diverted to the Cape of Good Hope, adding 10 to 12 days and substantial cost.'

e: note:'The Strait of Gibraltar is the exit from the Mediterranean into the Atlantic for all UK-bound crude routed via the Med. It receives three separate flows: Gulf crude arriving from Suez (8%), Kazakhstan CPC Blend arriving via the Bosphorus and Mediterranean (11%), and Libyan and Algerian crude loading directly into the Mediterranean (9%). All converge at Gibraltar before the final Atlantic leg to UK terminals. Gibraltar is wide (14km) and not classified as a strategic chokepoint, but it is the geographic confluence of the UK\'s most complex crude supply chains.'

e: note:'UK crude imports averaged approximately 850 thousand barrels per day in 2024. Primary receiving terminals: Milford Haven (Pembrokeshire), Hound Point (Firth of Forth), Teesside, Immingham, and Merseyside. UK domestic UKCS production has declined from a 1999 peak of 2.9 mb/d to under 700 kb/d; imports fill the gap. The UK is not a significant crude re-exporter.'
